title: The diagonal torus detects the scheme kernel of an SL2 representation
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $S=\operatorname{SL}_{2,k}$ be the affine group scheme whose $A$-points are the determinant-one $2\times2$ matrices over a commutative $k$-algebra $A$ [def-sc-group-scheme]. Let $D\subset S$ be its diagonal torus, $D(A)=\{\operatorname{diag}(s,s^{-1}):s\in A^\times\}$. If $N\subset S$ is a closed normal subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] with scheme-theoretic intersection $N\cap D=1$, then $N=1$. Here normal means stable under the conjugation morphism $S\times N\to S$, and the intersection is the fibre product of the two subgroup inclusions. Consequently, if $M$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space and $v:S\to\operatorname{GL}(M)$ is a group-scheme homomorphism whose restriction $v|_D$ is a closed immersion, then $v$ is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]. The conclusions hold in characteristic two as well as in every other characteristic, without any reducedness assumption on $N$.

source.place: Section 20g, pp.415--418, standard matrices of SL2 and its scalar centre; Theorem 3.34, p.75, for the closed-image conclusion. Agent-formulated kernel-detection lemma supporting Theorem 23.72; no assertion here is quoted as a theorem stated verbatim by Milne.

proof.text: Put $E=E_{12}$, $F=E_{21}$ and $H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. The tangent-space definition [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space] identifies $T_{N/k,1}$ with the subspace $W=\{X:I+\epsilon X\in N(k[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2)\}$ of trace-zero matrices: expanding the determinant gives $\det(I+\epsilon X)=1+\epsilon\operatorname{tr}X$, and the tangent operations are matrix addition and scalar multiplication. Normality makes $W$ stable under $X\mapsto gXg^{-1}$ for $g\in S(k)$. Moreover $W\cap kH=0$, since $I+\epsilon aH=\operatorname{diag}(1+\epsilon a,(1+\epsilon a)^{-1})$ belongs to $D(k[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2)$, so membership in $N$ forces it to be the identity by the scheme-intersection hypothesis.

source.place: Sections 10a--10c, dual-number tangent points (10.5--10.11 and 10.14), pp.186--190; agent matrix expansion. Tangent convention: Stacks Tag 0B2C, varieties-definition-tangent-space.

proof.text: The field $k$ is infinite: if it were finite, $\prod_{a\in k}(T-a)-1$ would be a nonconstant polynomial with no root. Choose $t_1,t_2,t_3\in k^\times$ whose squares $q_i=t_i^2$ are pairwise distinct, possible because a quadratic has at most two roots. For $X=aH+bE+cF\in W$, torus conjugation gives $aH+q_i bE+q_i^{-1}cF\in W$. The matrix with rows $(1,q_i,q_i^{-1})$ is invertible: multiplying row $i$ by $q_i$ and permuting columns gives the Vandermonde rows $(1,q_i,q_i^2)$, with determinant $\prod_{i<j}(q_j-q_i)\ne0$. Taking linear combinations shows $aH,bE,cF\in W$, and therefore $a=0$.

source.place: Sections 10b and 10d, formulas for dual-number points and conjugation, pp.188--193; elementary interpolation supplied by the agent.

proof.text: If $b\ne0$ for some $aH+bE+cF\in W$, step 2 gives $E\in W$. With $l=I+F\in S(k)$, direct multiplication gives $lEl^{-1}=E-H-F\in W$. Applying step 2 to this vector gives $-H\in W$, a contradiction. Similarly, $c\ne0$ would give $F\in W$, and $(I+E)F(I-E)=F+H-E$ would give $H\in W$. Thus $W=0$. In characteristic two $H=I_2$ is still nonzero, and its coefficient in both displayed conjugations is still a unit, so the same argument applies.

source.place: Section 10d, matrix formula Ad(A)(X)=AXA^{-1}, p.193, and Section 20g, p.415; explicit agent calculation.

proof.text: We next show $N(k)=\{I\}$. A scalar point of $N$ already lies in $D(k)$ and is the identity. If a nonscalar $n\in N(k)$ exists, choose a nonzero vector $v$ for which $nv\notin kv$: otherwise the two coordinate lines and the line through their sum would force $n$ to be scalar. Complete $v$ to a determinant-one basis by rescaling its second vector. Normality lets us replace $n$ by its matrix in this basis, whose lower-left entry $c$ is nonzero. Write the entries of $n$ as $a,b,c,d$ in row order, and put $u(t)=I+tE$. Then $z(t)=nu(t)n^{-1}u(-t)\in N(k)$, and multiplication using $ad-bc=1$ gives $\operatorname{tr}z(t)=2+c^2t^2$.

source.place: Section 20g, pp.415--416, elementary SL2 matrices; the trace calculation and choice of basis are supplied by the agent.

proof.text: Choose $t\in k$ with $(2+c^2t^2)^2\ne4$. This excludes only the roots of a nonzero degree-four polynomial (leading coefficient $c^4$), so step 2 ensures such a $t$ exists. Put $T=\operatorname{tr}z(t)$. The roots $\lambda,\lambda^{-1}$ of $x^2-Tx+1$ exist in $k$, are nonzero, and are distinct: a repeated root would have $\lambda^2=1$ and hence $T^2=4$, also in characteristic two. The two eigenvectors are linearly independent; rescaling one gives a determinant-one eigenbasis. Thus $z(t)$ is conjugate by $S(k)$ to $\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,\lambda^{-1})\ne I$. Normality puts this nonidentity diagonal point in $N(k)\cap D(k)$, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence $N(k)=\{I\}$.

source.place: Section 20g, pp.415--418; agent argument by the degree-two characteristic polynomial, with no classification theorem for normal subgroups.

proof.text: Since $N$ is closed in $S=\operatorname{Spec}k[a,b,c,d]/(ad-bc-1)$, the affine description of closed immersions [def-weil-closed-immersion] gives $N=\operatorname{Spec}B$ with $B$ a finitely generated $k$-algebra. It is Noetherian by [lem-wf-affine-noetherian-components]. Clause 1 of [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing] identifies its maximal ideals with its $k$-points. Step 5 therefore says that $B$ has exactly one maximal ideal, the augmentation ideal $\mathfrak m=\ker(B\to k)$ of the identity. Thus $B$ is local, its residue field is $k$, and $\mathfrak m$ is finitely generated. Neither this use of clause 1 nor the preceding steps assume that $B$ is reduced.

source.place: Section 1b, affine algebraic schemes, and Section 10a, identity tangent space; elementary application of the existing Noetherian and weak Nullstellensatz nodes.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sc-rational-tangent-cotangent-duality] to the rational identity of $\operatorname{Spec}B$ over $\operatorname{Spec}k$. Since $B$ is local its local ring there is $B$ itself; step 3 gives $0=W\cong\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2,k)$. The quotient is finite-dimensional because $\mathfrak m$ is finitely generated. If it were nonzero, extending a nonzero vector to a basis would give a nonzero functional, so $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2=0$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-nakayama-local-generators] with local ring $B$, module $\mathfrak m$ and the empty generating family: it generates the zero quotient, hence generates $\mathfrak m$. Therefore $\mathfrak m=0$, the augmentation is an isomorphism $B\simeq k$, and the identity section identifies $N$ with the trivial subgroup scheme.

source.place: Tag 0B2E, lemma-tangent-space-rational-point; Nakayama is algebra.tex Tag 00DV, lemma-NAK, item (8), as recorded by the existing local-generators node.

proof.text: For the consequence, let $K=\ker v$. By [lem-sc-kernel-subgroup] this is a closed subgroup scheme, with $K(A)=\ker(v_A)$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$. These kernels are normal, so conjugation restricts to $S\times K\to K$ (equivalently, the morphism to $\operatorname{GL}(M)$ is constantly the identity on that product). A closed immersion is injective on all algebra-valued points by its affine quotient description [def-weil-closed-immersion]; thus $v|_D$ has trivial kernel, and $K\cap D=1$. Steps 1--7 give $K=1$, hence $v_A$ is injective for every $A$. Both $S$ and $\operatorname{GL}(M)$ are affine of finite type: choose a basis of $M$ to use the determinant-coordinate presentation, and for $\dim M=0$ the target is the trivial affine group. Apply [lem-sfb-geometric-unipotence-faithful-closed-immersion] to conclude that $v$ is a closed immersion.

source.place: Corollary 3.35 and Theorem 3.34, printed p.75; the kernel and normality verification is by the displayed functor-of-points identity.
